text.p: A Mexican journalist whose newspaper is often critical of the government was abducted at gunpoint by masked men in the capital of southern Oaxaca state, colleagues said on Wednesday.
They said they held the government and security forces responsible for his life and well-being.
Razhy Gonzalez, founder and director of the alternative "Contrapunto" weekly newspaper, was seized near his offices late on Monday as he was walking with a friend.
The friend, who requested anonymity, told Reuters two men frisked Gonzalez at gunpoint and then bundled him into a car.
"They were waiting for us. They told me to go away. Their target was Razhy," she said in a phone interview.

"The journalists of Oaxaca ... hold the federal and state governments and the police forces responsible for the life and physical well-being of the journalist Razhy Gonzalez and demand his immediate appearance," a statement issued by his colleagues said.
In a letter to President Ernesto Zedillo, the New York-based Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) expressed its concern over the abduction.
"CPJ shares the concern among several of Gonzalez's colleagues that he may have been kidnapped because of his journalist work," the letter, a copy of which was faxed to Reuters, said.
A spokesman for the attorney general's office in the state capital Oaxaca said it had not been formally notified of the abduction, but that it was being investigated.

Gonzalez, whose newspaper has given wide coverage to social protests in the impoverished state, was one of a group of journalists taken to a clandestine meeting with a commander of the rebel Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) on Friday.
Gonzalez' friend said she doubted the captors were from the EPR.

The recently emerged EPR carried out a series of armed strikes in Oaxaca and several other states in late August in which at least 20 people were killed, mostly soldiers and police. The army has since stepped up counter-insurgency operations in the state.

"We believe this abduction, combined with a series of intimidations and obstacles to the work of providing information, only serves to worsen the grave situation the state is in," the statement by Oaxacan journalists said.

Since the EPR's appearance at the end of June, the government has clamped down on information about guerrilla attacks or activities, making it increasingly difficult to obtain reliable reports about what is happening in the remote parts of Mexico where the guerrillas operate.
